title: Todt tells Hitler: no victory

facts.text: On 29 November 1941 Fritz Todt, Reich Minister for Armaments and Munitions, met Hitler in the New Reich Chancellery in Berlin with the industrialist Walter Rohland.

Todt had run the armaments ministry since March 1940, after building the autobahns and founding the Organisation Todt, the construction force that came to use hundreds of thousands of forced labourers.
The stakes were stark. Rostov had just been lost, and the war economy had too little labour and raw materials for what the armed forces demanded for 1942.
Rohland had just come back from the Eastern Front, deeply impressed by the number and quality of Soviet tanks facing Army Group Centre.
According to Rohland's memoir, Todt told Hitler: "This war can no longer be won by military means." He argued that only a political solution was left.

Todt, a Nazi Party veteran, spoke with unusual candour. Counting growing Lend Lease deliveries from the United States, he said the enemy coalition could already turn out armoured vehicles so fast that a negotiated peace was unavoidable.
Hitler answered that the chances of such a peace were next to none. No transcript of the meeting survives; what was said comes from Rohland's later account.
Twelve days later, on 11 December 1941, Hitler declared war on the United States, the country whose factories Todt had warned about.

Todt raised the argument with Hitler again in the weeks that followed. The last time, on the night of 7 February 1942 at Hitler's headquarters near Rastenburg in East Prussia, the two men argued heatedly.
The next morning, 8 February, Todt's Heinkel He 111 crashed shortly after taking off from the Rastenburg airfield for Berlin, killing him and four others. Witnesses said it blew up in the air.
Albert Speer had accepted a seat on that flight but cancelled hours before, after a late night meeting with Hitler. That same day Hitler named Speer to succeed Todt.
An Air Ministry inquiry ruled out sabotage, but rumours of murder have never quite died. None has ever been proved.

photoNote: Tier: green. Studio portrait of Fritz Todt issued on his appointment as Reich Minister for Armaments and Munitions, 23 March 1940 (caption: Reichsminister Dr. Todt). Bundesarchiv Bild 146-1969-146-01, photographer Röhr (Weltbild; Commons also reads Röhn), CC BY-SA 3.0 de, via Wikimedia Commons. The Commons original is only 600 x 794; saved 960 x 1270 from the 960 px thumbnail, which Wikimedia upscales, so expect softness. A tight, serious face looking off frame suits a moment of doubt; he wears party uniform with collar tabs and ribbons along the bottom edge, so crop to the face and keep the framing neutral. A small photographer signature sits in the bottom right corner. There is no photo of the 29 November meeting. Runner up: Todt's coffin on a gun carriage on Unter den Linden, February 1942, Bundesarchiv Bild 183-J00405, 3813 px (better resolution, but it shows the ending, not the man).

declassified.fact: Todt was not the first to say it. About a month earlier General Friedrich Fromm, head of the army's General Office, had given Hitler's high command a virtually identical assessment of the war economy.
